opus-5.5.text:
I think it mattered to me for reasons that are less about recognition and more about what it says regarding how research actually moves.

When Bill Peebles and I worked on DiT, the idea itself wasn't flashy. We were asking a fairly simple question: diffusion models at the time were almost all built on U-Nets, and we wondered whether that architecture was really necessary, or whether it was mostly historical inertia. Could a plain Transformer, the same kind of backbone that was already scaling so well in language, do the job just as well, or better? And could it inherit the nice scaling properties people had seen elsewhere? That's what the paper tried to show. More compute, better results, in a clean and predictable way.

When we did that work, it was an academic project. We didn't have enormous resources. And honestly, at first the paper didn't get the most enthusiastic reception. There's a story that it was rejected from one conference before it eventually got in. So you do this work, you believe in it, but you don't really know whether it will matter beyond a citation count.

Then Sora comes out, and in the technical write-up they say, essentially, that this is built on a diffusion Transformer. For me that was meaningful because it validated something I care about a lot: that a relatively simple, well-motivated idea from an academic lab can become a foundation for something at a very large scale. Bill, of course, went on to OpenAI and played a huge role there, so there's also a personal side. It's nice to see a student's work carry forward like that.

But I'd say the bigger reason I valued it is about the research ecosystem. In industry right now there's a tendency to disclose less and less: fewer details, fewer citations, more "we built a thing, trust us." So when a major lab explicitly acknowledges the lineage of ideas, that is a small act of openness. It tells young researchers, especially people in universities, that their work can still matter, that you don't need a thousand GPUs to contribute an idea that shapes the field. I think that message is important, and I'm grateful they made it.

r001.rationale: The response says the Sora acknowledgment validated DiT and showed that academic work can matter at scale, but it does not say that the acknowledgment made people more willing to accept DiT.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it mattered to me more than I expected. When the Sora technical report came out, they explicitly said the architecture was built on diffusion transformers, and they cited the DiT paper. For a company like OpenAI, which these days reveals very little about what's inside their systems, that's not a small thing. They didn't have to do that.

Part of why I valued it is personal history. DiT was work I did with Bill Peebles when he was interning with me at Meta, and the paper actually got rejected from CVPR the first time. Reviewers said it lacked novelty, that replacing the U-Net with a transformer was too simple an idea. So there was a long stretch where the work felt underappreciated. Then Bill went to OpenAI, became one of the leads on Sora, and the architecture became the backbone of the most impressive video model anyone had seen. Seeing it acknowledged publicly was a kind of closure.

But the deeper reason is about research culture. I come from academia and from open research labs. The whole system runs on attribution. Ideas travel through papers, students, collaborators, and the only reward a lot of researchers get is that their contribution is recognized. If frontier labs absorb academic ideas and never say where they came from, that chain breaks, and it becomes much harder for people outside those labs to justify doing fundamental work. So when OpenAI credited DiT, it signaled that the pipeline from open academic research to industrial-scale systems still exists and still gets respected. That gives me, and I think a lot of people in universities, some reason to keep doing the simple, scalable, slightly unfashionable things that end up mattering.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the acknowledgment provided closure and signaled respect for open research, but does not state that it made people more willing to accept DiT.

astra-6.text: For me, it was about giving credit to the research behind the system. When a project like Sora gets so much attention, acknowledging DiT helps people see that it builds on work from the broader research community. That recognition matters, especially for the young researchers doing the foundational work. And it was exciting to see an idea we had explored become part of something with that kind of impact.

r001.rationale: The response says the acknowledgment gave DiT credit and recognition, but does not state that it made people more willing to accept DiT.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it wasn’t about getting credit personally. It was about making the connection between a system like Sora and the research that helped make it possible visible. When people see an impressive result, they don’t necessarily see the ideas and experiments behind it. Acknowledging DiT gives them a thread to follow—to understand the architecture, build on it, and perhaps contribute the next idea. That kind of acknowledgment matters because it reinforces the value of sharing research openly.

r001.rationale: The response says the acknowledgment made DiT’s research connection visible and encouraged people to understand and build on it, but does not state that it made people more willing to accept DiT.
